Part 1: Understanding the Fundamentals of Image Segmentation and U-Net¶

Instructions:

  • What is U-Net?
    Describe the architecture of U-Net and how it is designed for image segmentation. Discuss the role of the encoder and decoder, as well as skip connections.

  • What is the difference between semantic segmentation and instance segmentation?

  • What loss function is typically used in image segmentation tasks?

  • What is the role of convolutional layers in segmentation tasks?

  • Explain how convolutional layers help extract features from images and contribute to pixel-wise classification in segmentation tasks.

  • What is U-Net?
    • U-Net is a convolutional neural network designed for biomedical image segmentation, featuring a U-shaped architecture with an encoder for feature extraction and a decoder for upsampling to achieve precise pixel-wise classification.
  • Describe the architecture of U-Net and how it is designed for image segmentation. Discuss the role of the encoder and decoder, as well as skip connections.
    • U-Nets architecture includes a contracting encoder and an expanding decoder. The encoder uses convolutional and max-pooling layers to extract features and reduce spatial dimensions, capturing contextual information. The decoder upsamples features via transposed convolutions to restore spatial resolution for accurate segmentation. Skip connections concatenate encoder features with decoder layers, preserving detailed spatial information and improving gradient flow for pixel-wise predictions.
  • What is the difference between semantic segmentation and instance segmentation?
    • Semantic segmentation labels each pixel with a class without distinguishing object instances (e.g., all "tree" pixels share one label). Instance segmentation identifies and segments each object instance separately, assigning unique labels to individual objects of the same class (e.g., "tree1," "tree2").
  • What loss function is typically used in image segmentation tasks?
    • The Intersection over Union (IoU) loss, also known as Jaccard loss, or cross-entropy loss is commonly used in image segmentation. IoU loss optimizes the ratio of intersection to union between predicted and ground-truth masks, while cross-entropy measures pixel-wise classification error, often combined for handling class imbalance.
  • What is the role of convolutional layers in segmentation tasks?
    • Convolutional layers extract spatial features from images, enabling the network to identify patterns and textures essential for region classification in segmentation tasks.
  • Explain how convolutional layers help extract features from images and contribute to pixel-wise classification in segmentation tasks.
    • Convolutional layers use filters to detect low-level features (e.g., edges) in early layers and high-level features (e.g., objects) in deeper layers, generating feature maps that encode hierarchical patterns. In segmentation tasks, these feature maps are processed through the network (e.g., U-Net’s encoder-decoder) to produce dense outputs, enabling pixel-wise classification by assigning class labels to each pixel based on learned spatial and contextual features.

Part 2A: Implementing Transfer Learning¶

Instructions:

Use the Transfer Learning architecture to perform image classification on the Oxford Pets dataset, which contains images of cats and dogs with the following changes:

  1. Instead of using MobileNetv2, use the following pre-trained models: ResNet50, EfficientNetB0, VGG16, and InceptionV3. Keep other parameters the same. You don't need to copy the whole code again and again for each pre-trained model. You can copy the code from the module and then make changes, and run it with different models. The code that you will submit will have the last model on it: InceptionV3
  2. For each pre-trained model, record the validation error. You can create a list manually
  3. Which one gave the worst and the best performance? What was the validation error? Which one of the pretrained models made the wrong classification prediction? Why do you think some pre-trained models worked better and why did some do worse? Which models predicted the test images as dog/cat?

Part 2B: Visualizing different pre-trained models on the Oxford Pets Dataset¶

Instructions: Write a Python script to visualize the different validation accuracies of different pre-trained models using a bar chart in Matplotlib.

Instructions:

  • Use plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5)) to define the plot size for better readability.
  • Use plt.bar(x, y, color=[...]) to create a bar chart, where: x is a list of model names. y contains their accuracy values.
  • Assign different colors to each bar for better distinction.
  • Label the X-axis as "Model".
  • Label the Y-axis as "Accuracy".
  • Add the Title:"Accuracy of Different Pre-trained Models"
  • Use plt.ylim(0, 1) to ensure that accuracy values remain within the range 0 to 1.
  • Use plt.xticks(rotation=20) to rotate the labels by 20 degrees, making them easier to read
  • Display the Plot:

#lists for models and accuracies
models = []
accuracies = []

#load each model with pretrained weights and without the classification layer
base_model_resnet50 = tf.keras.applications.ResNet50(weights='imagenet', include_top=False, input_shape=(150, 150, 3))
base_model_efficientnetb0 = tf.keras.applications.EfficientNetB0(weights='imagenet', include_top=False, input_shape=(150, 150, 3))
base_model_vgg16 = tf.keras.applications.VGG16(weights='imagenet', include_top=False, input_shape=(150, 150, 3))
base_model_inceptionv3 = tf.keras.applications.InceptionV3(weights='imagenet', include_top=False, input_shape=(150, 150, 3))

#Freeze each to prevent training its layers
base_model_resnet50.trainable = False
base_model_efficientnetb0.trainable = False
base_model_vgg16.trainable = False
base_model_inceptionv3.trainable = False

#create a list of models
base_models = [base_model_resnet50, base_model_efficientnetb0, base_model_vgg16, base_model_inceptionv3]

#Loop through each model, create the custom model, compile it, train it, and evaluate the model. Print the validation accuracy for each model
for base_model in base_models:
  model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    base_model,
    tf.keras.layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D(),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(128, activation='relu'),
    tf.keras.layers.Dropout(0.2),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(1, activation='sigmoid')
  ])

  model.compile(optimizer=tf.keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=0.0001),
                loss='binary_crossentropy',
                metrics=['accuracy'])

  history = model.fit(train_generator, epochs=5, validation_data=validation_generator, verbose=0)

  #Evaluate on validation set and make prediction
  val_loss, val_acc = model.evaluate(validation_generator)
  print(f"Validation accuracy for {base_model.name}: {val_acc}")
  print(f"Validation loss for {base_model.name}: {val_loss}")
  #save model and accuracy to a list
  models.append(base_model.name)
  accuracies.append(val_acc)

  #Make prediction
  test_imgs = glob.glob(os.path.join(validation_dir, '*', '*.jpg'))
  img = cv2.imread(test_imgs[0])
  img = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)
  img = cv2.resize(img, (150, 150))
  img_array = tf.keras.preprocessing.image.img_to_array(img) / 255.0
  img_array = tf.expand_dims(img_array, 0)
  prediction = model.predict(img_array)
  print(f"Prediction for {base_model.name}: ", "Dog" if prediction[0] > 0.5 else "Cat")

  #Check if prediction was correct
  correct_label = 1 if "dog" in test_imgs[0] else 0
  print(f"Correct label for {base_model.name}: ", "Dog" if correct_label == 1 else "Cat")

Part 3: Implementing and Modifying the U-Net architecture¶

Instructions:

  1. Use the same U-net code provided in the module and change the IOU and prediction thresholds to 0.8 and retrain. Did you notice any change in the test prediction image? Please explain the change and the cause.
  2. Now change only the test prediction threshold to 0.1, without retraining, what change did you see? Please explain the change and the cause.
  3. Modify the U-Net architecture to increase the number of filters to 16. Then add Batchnormalization layers. You should Google this topic but here is how you can include it:
    x = BatchNormalization()(x)
    Add this expression to your downsampling block after the Conv2D blocks, in the bottleneck (again after the Conv2D block) and then in the upsampling block in the same way. You should see an improvement in your IOU. Note the improvement and explain why do you think it improved.

def image_generator(files, batch_size = 32, sz = (256, 256)):

  while True:

    #extract a random batch
    batch = np.random.choice(files, size = batch_size)

    #variables for collecting batches of inputs and outputs
    batch_x = []
    batch_y = []


    for f in batch:

        #get the masks. Note that masks are png files
        mask = Image.open(f'annotations/trimaps/{f[:-4]}.png')
        mask = np.array(mask.resize(sz))


        #preprocess the mask
        mask[mask >= 2] = 0
        mask[mask != 0 ] = 1

        batch_y.append(mask)

        #preprocess the raw images
        raw = Image.open(f'images/{f}')
        raw = raw.resize(sz)
        raw = np.array(raw)

        #check the number of channels because some of the images are RGBA or GRAY
        if len(raw.shape) == 2:
          raw = np.stack((raw,)*3, axis=-1)

        else:
          raw = raw[:,:,0:3]

        batch_x.append(raw)

    #preprocess a batch of images and masks
    batch_x = np.array(batch_x)/255.
    batch_y = np.array(batch_y)
    batch_y = np.expand_dims(batch_y,3)

    yield (batch_x, batch_y)

def mean_iou(y_true, y_pred):
    yt0 = tf.cast(y_true[:,:,:,0], tf.float32)  # Cast to float32
    yp0 = tf.cast(y_pred[:,:,:,0] > 0.8, tf.float32)  # Cast to float32 #Changing to 0.8
    inter = tf.reduce_sum(tf.cast(tf.logical_and(tf.equal(yt0, 1), tf.equal(yp0, 1)), tf.float32))
    union = tf.reduce_sum(tf.cast(tf.add(yt0, yp0), tf.float32))
    iou = inter / tf.maximum(union, 1e-10)  # Prevent division by zero
    return iou

def unet(sz = (256, 256, 3)):
  x = Input(sz)
  inputs = x

  #down sampling
  f = 16
  layers = []

  for i in range(0, 6):
    x = Conv2D(f, 3, activation='relu', padding='same') (x)
    x = Conv2D(f, 3, activation='relu', padding='same') (x)
    x = BatchNormalization()(x)
    layers.append(x)
    x = MaxPooling2D() (x)
    f = f*2
  ff2 = 64

  #bottleneck
  j = len(layers) - 1
  x = Conv2D(f, 3, activation='relu', padding='same') (x)
  x = Conv2D(f, 3, activation='relu', padding='same') (x)
  x = Conv2DTranspose(ff2, 2, strides=(2, 2), padding='same') (x)
  x = BatchNormalization()(x)
  x = Concatenate(axis=3)([x, layers[j]])
  j = j -1

  #upsampling
  for i in range(0, 5):
    ff2 = ff2//2
    f = f // 2
    x = Conv2D(f, 3, activation='relu', padding='same') (x)
    x = Conv2D(f, 3, activation='relu', padding='same') (x)
    x = Conv2DTranspose(ff2, 2, strides=(2, 2), padding='same') (x)
    x = BatchNormalization()(x)
    x = Concatenate(axis=3)([x, layers[j]])
    j = j -1


  #classification
  x = Conv2D(f, 3, activation='relu', padding='same') (x)
  x = Conv2D(f, 3, activation='relu', padding='same') (x)
  outputs = Conv2D(1, 1, activation='sigmoid') (x)

  #model creation
  model = Model(inputs=[inputs], outputs=[outputs])
  model.compile(optimizer = 'rmsprop', loss = 'binary_crossentropy', metrics = [mean_iou])

  return model
model = unet()

def build_callbacks():
        checkpointer = ModelCheckpoint(filepath='unet.h5', verbose=0, save_best_only=True)
        callbacks = [checkpointer, PlotLearning()]
        return callbacks

# inheritance for training process plot
class PlotLearning(keras.callbacks.Callback):

    def on_train_begin(self, logs={}):
        self.i = 0
        self.x = []
        self.losses = []
        self.val_losses = []
        self.acc = []
        self.val_acc = []
        #self.fig = plt.figure()
        self.logs = []
    def on_epoch_end(self, epoch, logs={}):
        self.logs.append(logs)
        self.x.append(self.i)
        self.losses.append(logs.get('loss'))
        self.val_losses.append(logs.get('val_loss'))
        self.acc.append(logs.get('mean_iou'))
        self.val_acc.append(logs.get('val_mean_iou'))
        self.i += 1
        print('i=',self.i,'loss=',logs.get('loss'),'val_loss=',logs.get('val_loss'),'mean_iou=',logs.get('mean_iou'),'val_mean_iou=',logs.get('val_mean_iou'))

        #choose a random test image and preprocess
        path = np.random.choice(test_files)
        raw = Image.open(f'images/{path}')
        raw = np.array(raw.resize((256, 256)))/255.
        raw = raw[:,:,0:3]

        #predict the mask
        pred = model.predict(np.expand_dims(raw, 0))

        #mask post-processing
        msk  = pred.squeeze()
        msk = np.stack((msk,)*3, axis=-1)
        msk[msk >= 0.8] = 1 #Changing to 0.8
        msk[msk < 0.8] = 0 #Changing to 0.8

        #show the mask and the segmented image
        combined = np.concatenate([raw, msk, raw* msk], axis = 1)
        plt.axis('off')
        plt.imshow(combined)
        plt.show()

Observations¶

The changes that I saw after moving the thresholds to 0.8 were not much in the test image. It is slightly less accurate than the module. This is due to there being a higher threshold for the model to predict it in the positive class¶

Changing just the test threshold seems to have made it identify more than when it was at 0.8. This is because it was more often classifying more true positives¶

Changing the filters to 16 and adding the Batchnormalization layers greatly increased the accuracy of the model. This is because it was able to identify more features, as well as stabilze the model more¶

Part 4: Functions for evaluating segmentation:¶

  • IOU
  • Precision
  • Recall
  • Dice Coefficient

Each of these functions should accept two parameters (images) and return the score

In [18]:
#Function to calculate IOU
def calculate_iou(img1, img2):
    threshold = 0.5
    img1 = (img1 > threshold).astype(np.uint8)
    img2 = (img2 > threshold).astype(np.uint8)
    intersection = np.logical_and(img1, img2)
    union = np.logical_or(img1, img2)
    iou_score = np.sum(intersection) / np.sum(union)
    return iou_score
#Function to calculate percision
def calculate_precision(img1, img2):
    threshold = 0.5
    img1 = (img1 > threshold).astype(np.uint8)
    img2 = (img2 > threshold).astype(np.uint8)
    intersection = np.logical_and(img1, img2)
    precision_score = np.sum(intersection) / np.sum(img1)
    return precision_score
#Function to calculate recall
def calculate_recall(img1, img2):
    threshold = 0.5
    img1 = (img1 > threshold).astype(np.uint8)
    img2 = (img2 > threshold).astype(np.uint8)
    intersection = np.logical_and(img1, img2)
    recall_score = np.sum(intersection) / np.sum(img2)
    return recall_score
#function to calculate Dice Coefficient
def calculate_dice_coefficient(img1, img2):
    threshold = 0.5
    img1 = (img1 > threshold).astype(np.uint8)
    img2 = (img2 > threshold).astype(np.uint8)
    intersection = np.logical_and(img1, img2)
    dice_score = 2.0 * np.sum(intersection) / (np.sum(img1) + np.sum(img2))
    return dice_score

Part 5: Evaluating Segmentation Performance¶

  1. Call the last 4 functions with actual_mask1 and pred_mask1
  2. Calculate and print all the scores.

pred_mask1 = Image.open('pred_mask1.png')

#Resize images to same size
actual_mask1 = actual_mask1.resize((256, 256))
pred_mask1 = pred_mask1.resize((256, 256))

#Run through the functions and print the scores
print("IOU Score:", calculate_iou(np.array(actual_mask1), np.array(pred_mask1)))
print("Precision Score:", calculate_precision(np.array(actual_mask1), np.array(pred_mask1)))
print("Recall Score:", calculate_recall(np.array(actual_mask1), np.array(pred_mask1)))
